column2: At six o’clock, the city began to change. The shops were closing. Metal doors came down with a crash. Buses filled with tired people, and the streets grew dark beneath the evening sky. Daniel walked slowly along the pavement. He did not look behind him. He did not need to. He could feel someone there.

A man stood beside a red phone box. He wore a grey coat and held a newspaper open in front of his face. Daniel had seen him near the station. Or had he? The man turned a page. Daniel turned left. There was no reason to turn left. The street was narrow and almost empty. A sign above a shop moved in the wind, making a small, sharp noise. Daniel stopped. The noise stopped too. He began to walk again.

His shoes made a soft sound on the wet pavement. He tried to walk like everyone else, but every person seemed to have a reason to be there. A woman hurried past with a bag held close to her body. A boy stood near a street light, looking at his phone. An old man sat on a bench with his hands folded. They were all doing something. The woman might be carrying a message. The boy might be watching him. The old man might be waiting for someone. Daniel looked at the old man’s hands. They were still. Too still.

A bus pulled up beside the pavement. Its doors opened with a hiss. People climbed on. Daniel stayed where he was. Through the windows, he saw a man in a blue hat. The man looked at him once, then turned away. Daniel watched the bus move into the traffic. Its red lights grew smaller and smaller. For a moment, he felt safer. Then he noticed the blue hat in the window of a café. The man was sitting inside.

Daniel crossed the road. A car horn sounded behind him. He jumped, then kept walking. The driver shouted something, but Daniel did not turn around. He reached the other side and went into a crowded market. The market was full of voices. A woman called out the price of apples. A child cried beside a stall. Somewhere, a radio played an old song. The sounds mixed together until Daniel could not hear any one of them clearly. That was better. Noise could hide him.

He moved between the stalls. A man sold bright scarves. Another man cut bread with a long knife. Near the back, a girl was arranging flowers in a metal bucket. Daniel passed her, then stopped. She had placed one white flower on top of the others. The flower faced him. He walked on.

At the end of the market, he entered a quiet street. The windows were dark. A cat sat on a wall and watched him pass. Daniel looked back at the market entrance. Nobody came out. Perhaps there had never been anyone following him. The thought made him feel worse. If he was alone, then why was he so afraid?

A door opened somewhere behind him. Daniel turned. A woman stepped out of a building and held a small parcel against her chest. She looked at him. He looked at her. Neither of them spoke. Then she walked quickly towards the main road. Daniel watched until she disappeared. The parcel could contain anything.

At the next corner, a traffic light changed from red to green. Daniel crossed, even though no cars were coming. On the other side, a tall building rose above the street. Its many windows reflected the last light of the day. Daniel saw his own face in the glass: pale, tired, unfamiliar. Behind his reflection, something moved. He turned around. A bicycle leaned against a wall. Its front wheel was slowly turning. There was no wind now. Daniel stared at the wheel until it stopped. He began to walk faster.

The streets became smaller. He passed a bakery with its lights still on. Warm air came through the open door, carrying the smell of fresh bread. For one moment, the smell reminded him of home. His sister used to buy bread on Friday evenings. She would bring it back in a paper bag and break it into pieces while it was still warm. Daniel almost went inside. Then a man at the counter looked up. The man’s eyes stayed on Daniel for a little too long. Daniel moved away from the door. The smell of bread faded behind him.

At the end of the street, he found a station entrance. People went down the steps in a steady line. Daniel joined them. Their coats brushed against his. Someone’s bag knocked his leg. A child laughed. Daniel kept his eyes on the steps. Below ground, the air was hot and close. The station lights made every face look pale. A train waited on the platform with its doors open. Daniel stepped inside.

He chose a seat near the door. Across from him, a young man wore a black scarf. Beside him, a woman held a red umbrella. At the far end, a worker carried a large box. Daniel looked at each of them. The young man’s shoes were clean. The woman’s umbrella was dry, although it had been raining. The worker’s box was open at one corner. Small things. Nothing important. The doors began to close. A hand appeared between them. The doors opened again, and a man stepped inside. He wore a grey coat.

Daniel stood up. The man took the seat he had just left. He folded his hands. His face was calm. The train started moving. Daniel held the metal pole. The lights passed over the windows, making the dark outside appear and disappear. A tunnel wall. A bright sign. A face in the glass. His own face again, with the grey-coated man just behind it. Daniel shut his eyes.

The train slowed. A recorded voice named the next station. The doors opened. People moved towards the exit. Daniel waited until the last moment, then stepped onto the platform. He walked quickly up the stairs and out into the night. The city was colder now. Rain touched his face. The streets shone beneath the lamps. Daniel looked across the road. The man in the grey coat was not there.

He looked towards the station entrance. The doors opened for a group of people. No grey coat. Then, in a shop window, Daniel saw a shape standing behind him. He turned. A poster covered the wall. It showed a man in a grey coat, looking straight ahead. Daniel moved closer. The poster was old and wet. One corner had come loose and lifted in the wind. It was only paper. Daniel told himself this as he walked away. It was only a poster. It was only a shadow. It was only a man in a coat. But the city was full of windows. And every window held a face.

The football ground looked smaller than Noah had expected. From the bus, it had seemed to stretch across the whole hill. Now he stood at the gate with his kit bag cutting into his shoulder. Beyond the fence, boys in bright shirts ran across the wet grass. Their shouts rose into the cold air, then broke apart.

Noah’s hands were already damp. He wiped them on his shorts, although he had not started running yet. In his bag, his boots were wrapped in an old towel. His mother had given it to him that morning. “For luck,” she had said. She did not really believe in luck, but she had said it kindly, and he had smiled.

At the gate, a man in a green jacket checked his name. “Noah Bell?” He nodded. The man pointed towards a group near the far touchline. Noah thanked him and walked across the ground. He tried not to look at the other players. Their legs seemed longer. Their voices seemed stronger. One boy was laughing so loudly that everyone nearby turned to listen.

Noah changed behind a small building with peeling white paint. He took off his school clothes carefully and folded them into his bag. Then he sat down to tie his boots. He pulled each lace tight, loosened it, and pulled it tight again. His fingers were shaking. He pressed both palms against his knees and waited for them to stop.

When he joined the group, the coach gave a short welcome. There would be running, passing and a small match. The coach spoke as if this were an ordinary afternoon. Perhaps it was for him. For Noah, the next hour had been growing larger in his mind for weeks. He had imagined every mistake. He had imagined the coach watching him fail.

The first run began with a whistle. Noah moved quickly, his breath sharp in his chest. The grass was soft beneath his boots. He passed two players on the way to the line, then turned and ran back. His legs felt heavy at first. By the third run, the tight feeling in his stomach had started to loosen.

They practised passing in pairs. Noah was matched with a tall boy called Ethan, who hardly looked at him. The first ball came too fast. Noah stopped it with the side of his foot and sent it back. Their next passes were cleaner. Soon the ball moved between them without either boy needing to speak. Noah began to notice the space around him.

Then came the small match. Noah was placed on the left side. At first, he stayed close to the line and waited for the ball. The game moved quickly. Players called out. Boots struck the ground. A boy fell and got up again without looking at anyone. Noah felt the old fear return: he would be forgotten, standing at the edge while the game carried on without him.

He watched the other players instead of watching the ball. One defender kept turning his head towards the middle. Each time he did, the space behind him opened for a moment. Noah saw it twice. The second time, he moved into it. A pass came across the grass, and he took the ball forward before the defender could turn around.

The ball stayed close to his feet. Noah heard someone shout, but the sound seemed to come from far away. The goal stood ahead of him, white and quiet. He could have tried to shoot. Instead, he saw a teammate running in from the middle. Noah passed the ball across. The boy struck it once, and it went into the corner of the net.

For a second, Noah did not move. Then his teammate raised a hand, and Noah raised his own. Nobody made a speech. The game started again. Still, something inside him had changed. He had seen the space. He had trusted what he saw. The pass had been simple, but he had made it at the right moment.

Near the end, the other team attacked. Noah ran back and reached the ball just before their forward. He did not kick it away. He turned his body between the player and the ball, then passed it towards the middle. His heart was beating hard enough to hurt. The coach, standing beside the pitch, made a small mark on his paper.

When the whistle ended the match, the players gathered near the coach. Noah listened while the man spoke about effort and teamwork. He could hear his own breathing. His shirt clung to his back, and mud marked one knee. The coach said they would contact everyone later in the week. Noah nodded, though he knew he would spend every day waiting.

He changed slowly behind the building. His fingers were no longer shaking. When he pulled off his boots, grass stuck to the soles. He cleaned it away with the corner of the towel his mother had given him. The towel was damp now, but it still smelled faintly of washing powder. He folded it and put it back in the bag.

Outside the gate, he stopped and looked across the pitch. The players had gone. The coach was collecting cones, one at a time. Noah’s legs ached, and his mouth tasted of cold air. But his thoughts were clear. He had run when he was tired. He had found space. He had made a pass that mattered.

On the bus home, Noah sat by the window with his bag on his knees. The city moved past in grey walls and shop lights. He thought about the goal, then about the way he had protected the ball near the end. A smile came before he could stop it. His eyes grew hot. He blinked, embarrassed, though nobody was watching.

He was proud of himself. The feeling was quiet but strong, like a light left on in a room. He did not know whether the coach would choose him. He could not control that. But he knew what he had done out there, and he did not need anyone else to tell him it had been good.

In March, the river begins to wake. Rain runs down from the hills, and the last snow melts in the high places. Water slips between the stones, then joins the stream below. The river grows wider each day. It carries bits of earth and broken twigs, stirring up the dark soil at the bottom.

Along its banks, the trees are still bare. Their thin branches reach over the water like fingers. Then, one morning, the first green leaves appear. They are small and bright, almost too delicate to touch. More follow each day until the river runs beneath a soft roof of green.

The water is full of life again. It moves quickly, carrying food from the hills and spreading it through the valley. In the shallows, tiny plants begin to grow between the stones. The river’s surface shines in the changing light. Even on a cloudy day, it seems to hold a little of the sky.

New lives appear all around it. A mother duck guides a line of small, yellow ducklings along the bank. In a nest above the water, young birds call for food. Their voices are thin but steady. Near the reeds, a rabbit lifts its head, listens, then disappears into the grass with its young.

By late spring, the river has settled into its banks. The trees are covered in leaves, and their shadows move over the water. The air smells of wet earth and fresh grass. Small insects hover above the surface. When one touches the water, a fish rises with a quick splash, leaving circles that spread and fade.

Summer comes slowly, then all at once. The days grow long and warm. Sunlight rests on the river from morning until evening, turning the shallows gold. Children’s voices sometimes drift from the path, but the water keeps its own steady sound. It slides past the stones, bright and busy beneath the heat.

The river is full of fish now. They move beneath the surface, quick flashes of silver and brown. Some hide in the cool pools where the water runs deep. Others gather near the banks, among roots and weeds. A patient heron stands nearby, still as a post, waiting for the right moment.

The trees give shade to the animals along the bank. Bees travel between flowers, and dragonflies skim above the reeds. On hot afternoons, the river seems to slow. Its surface hardly moves in the wide pools. But under the calm shine, the current is always going somewhere, carrying the warmth of summer downstream.

In August, the sun begins to set earlier. The change is small at first. One evening, the light leaves the hills before dinner. A cool breeze moves through the trees, and a few leaves turn yellow near the path. The river notices the change in the air, though it still runs warm beneath the fading light.

Autumn reaches the valley in colours. Yellow spreads across the trees, then orange and red. Leaves break free and drift down, landing on the water. Some float for a while, turning slowly in the current. Others gather beside the bank, where the river catches them and holds them against the stones.

The air grows sharper. The fish move into deeper water, where the cold arrives more slowly. Birds travel in groups above the valley, calling to one another as they go. Along the bank, animals search for food. The rabbit’s young are larger now, and they know the paths between the grass and the trees.

Rain returns, tapping on the leaves and darkening the earth. The river rises a little and pushes around the fallen branches. Its water becomes brown again, carrying soil from the hills. Yet autumn does not make the river wild. It moves with quiet strength, gathering what the season gives and taking it onwards.

By winter, most of the leaves are gone. The trees stand bare against a grey sky. The river is darker now, and its banks are empty. A thin mist rests above the water on cold mornings. From the path, the valley seems still. Even the birds are quiet, hidden among the branches or far away.

On the coldest days, ice forms at the river’s edge. It holds the reeds in place and shines like glass. The middle of the river keeps moving. Beneath the grey surface, fish rest in deep pools. Seeds lie under the soil, and small animals sleep in warm nests. Life has grown quiet, but it has not disappeared.

Winter lasts longer than the other seasons seem to. Then, one afternoon, rain falls softly instead of freezing. A line of water slips from a hill and joins the river. The current quickens around a stone. On a bare branch, a small green bud opens. The river carries the new rain into the valley, ready to begin again.
